item.title: Byte-sized — Friday, 17 July
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized. It's Friday, the seventeenth of July, and today we've got six sections lined up: Japan and Asia-Pacific, A.I. and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community, events and marketing, and one interesting thing to close us out. Let's get into it.
Starting with Japan and Asia-Pacific. Japan's parliament has passed amendments to the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act that reclassify crypto as a financial product, putting it in the same regulatory bucket as stocks and bonds rather than treating it as a payment method. The reform brings insider trading rules, mandatory disclosures for issuers and prison terms of up to ten years for unregistered operators, alongside a flat tax rate on crypto gains of around twenty percent, down from as high as fifty five percent under the old rules. It takes effect around January twenty twenty eight, and the Japan Exchange Group is already eyeing domestic spot crypto exchange traded funds as early as twenty twenty seven, a sign Tokyo wants to be seen as a serious, well regulated home for digital assets rather than a cautionary tale.
Over in India, two stories point the same way: state governments are competing hard for capital. Gujarat has unveiled a data centre policy for the next three years targeting sixty two billion, seven hundred seventy million dollars in investment and seven and a half gigawatts of capacity, while Uttar Pradesh has approved its own new startup policy alongside a matching data centre policy of its own. It is the kind of state-by-state industrial policy race that rarely makes international headlines but shapes where the next wave of Asian data infrastructure actually gets built.
And in Washington, a new analysis from CSIS's India chair argues that the long-stalled first tranche of the U.S.-India bilateral trade agreement could finally move, once two ongoing American trade investigations wrap up and a ten percent global tariff imposed by the Trump administration expires on the twenty fourth of July. The piece is candid that the relationship has more often suffered from too many overlapping dialogue channels than too few, and argues this pause is a chance to simplify them rather than simply resume business as usual.
Now, over to A.I. and tech, where the biggest release of the week comes from Thinking Machines, the lab founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati. It has published its first open-weight model, called Inkling, a mixture of experts system with nine hundred seventy five billion total parameters, forty one billion of them active at any one time, multimodal reasoning across text, images and audio, and a context window of a million tokens. Releasing a model of that scale as open weights, rather than keeping it behind an API, is a statement in itself about how the newer labs plan to compete with the incumbents.
OpenAI, meanwhile, has shipped its first piece of branded hardware, and it is deliberately small. Codex Micro is a two hundred thirty dollar mechanical keypad built with a company called Work Louder, designed to let developers steer coding agents with physical keys rather than a keyboard shortcut, complete with a joystick for switching between tasks like code review and debugging and a dial for adjusting how much the model reasons before it acts. It is not the consumer smart speaker that OpenAI's hardware chief, former Apple design lead Jony Ive, is reportedly building, but arriving the same week Apple sued OpenAI over trade secrets tied to that unreleased device, the timing was hard to miss.
Elsewhere, the workflow orchestration company Prefect is acquiring rival Dagster, absorbing around forty staff while promising to keep Dagster's name, pricing and product roadmap intact for now, another sign that the crowded data pipeline tooling market is starting to consolidate. And a growing theme across this week's developer newsletters is what people are calling self-improving harnesses: frameworks that let an AI agent analyse its own execution traces and rewrite the scaffolding it operates inside. One widely shared experiment ran a coding agent on itself for eight days and came away with a smaller, faster prompt and a system that had quietly out-performed a harness engineers had spent two years hand-tuning, which is either an efficiency breakthrough or a reason to pay closer attention to what these systems are doing unsupervised, depending on your mood. In a related vein, Perplexity has detailed a sandbox platform called Space, which spins up an isolated, disposable environment for every task an AI agent handles and destroys it afterwards, isolating credentials and encrypting storage along the way, the kind of unglamorous infrastructure that becomes essential the moment agents are trusted with anything sensitive.
Now, over to startups and venture, where European robotics had a genuinely big day. Aramco Ventures, the venture arm of the Saudi oil and gas giant, is in talks to back the London humanoid robotics startup Humanoid in a deal that could value the company at around one point one to one point two billion dollars on roughly two hundred million dollars raised, while Amsterdam-based Monumental, which builds robots for construction sites, closed a thirty two million dollar Series B led by Khosla Ventures. European investors have already ploughed two point seven billion euros into robotics this year against one and a half billion for the whole of last year, and founders in the space are increasingly framing robotics, rather than software, as the continent's best shot at building globally relevant technology companies.
Lenny's Newsletter flagged a compensation trend worth knowing if you are hiring or being hired at that level: so-called builder executives, the operators who can still personally ship product, are starting to get paid like professional athletes, with pay packages that reward hands-on building ability rather than pure management scope for the first time in a long while.
And on the bootstrapped end of the spectrum, Indie Hackers profiled Saeed Ezzati, who built a Chrome extension called Superpower ChatGPT in a couple of days during the first week ChatGPT launched because he found the native interface clunky. He kept it free for nine months, funded it through a companion newsletter, and now runs it solo to four hundred twenty thousand downloads, one hundred fifty thousand weekly active users and five figures in monthly recurring revenue, a useful reminder that some of the best founder stories are still just one person fixing their own problem in public.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics, where CSIS trade expert Bill Reinsch has a sharp column on what he calls the trade transparency challenge. As supply chains have become genuinely global, with components sourced from dozens of countries before final assembly somewhere else entirely, determining a product's true country of origin has become far harder just as governments are demanding far more of that information for security reasons. His conclusion is blunt: more due diligence for manufacturers and customs brokers, more contested origin disputes for lawyers to argue over, and ultimately higher prices for consumers.
And on Ukraine, CSIS's Futures Lab frames the war as a race between two competing theories of victory. Kyiv is betting on maximising drone production and cheap, high-payoff deep strikes, backed by AI and integrated with cyber and electronic warfare, aimed at Russia's oil and gas revenue. Moscow is betting on a punishment campaign against critical infrastructure and political centres like Kyiv itself, hoping to force a settlement on its own terms. The analysts argue that whichever deep strike campaign proves more sustainable over the next six months, not the static front line, is now the most likely thing to actually end the war, which is a useful corrective for anyone still picturing this conflict mainly in terms of trenches and territory.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, where the idea worth stealing is about how founders run board meetings. The newsletter The VC Corner argues that most founders waste their board's time walking through thirty slides live, when the better approach is sending a tight packet four to five days ahead of the meeting so nobody is surprised by the numbers, then spending the actual hour on the two or three decisions only the board can make. It is a small operational shift, but one that changes a board meeting from a status update people endure into a working session people actually value.
And Marketing Brew looked at how the crisps brand Lay's approached World Cup marketing this summer, leaning into bandwagon fandom rather than pretending to have deep footballing credibility. Instead of chasing authenticity it cannot claim, the brand built campaigns around the casual, join-in-for-the-spectacle fans who only pay attention once every four years, a reminder that leaning into what your audience actually is can beat pretending to be something you are not.
Finally, one interesting thing to take you into the day. The newsletter Every has a timely piece questioning one of this year's more fashionable AI habits: building ever larger libraries of custom skills, the reusable instruction packages that load automatically when an AI assistant thinks they are relevant. On parts of the internet, a sprawling skill library has become something people show off, but the piece argues that stacking in skills indiscriminately can just as easily clutter an agent's context and make its answers worse, not better. The lesson, as with most tools, is that skills only help when you reach for them deliberately, not simply because you can.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and I'll see you back here tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Wednesday, 15 July
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized. It's Wednesday, the fifteenth of July, and today we've got six sections lined up: Japan and Asia-Pacific, A.I. and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community, events and marketing, and one interesting thing to close us out. Let's get into it.
Starting with Japan and Asia-Pacific. Fukuoka Now's weekly roundup has Kyushu heading into summer with a burst of local activity. Kitakyushu is launching a free transit campaign from the seventeenth of July, offering free rides on buses, trains and the monorail to encourage residents to explore more of their own city. Meanwhile roadside land values kept climbing across the region, up over four percent in Fukuoka Prefecture and even more in neighbouring Saga, a sign that the postpandemic property recovery in regional Japan still has legs. And Japan Airlines has teamed up with JR Kyushu, Kumamoto Airport and the Kyushu Tourism Organisation on their first joint international campaign to pull in more overseas visitors, a coordinated push that says as much about inbound tourism strategy as any single headline number does.
Elsewhere in the region, Google Cloud is expanding its partnership with Samsung Electronics, rolling out its Gemini Enterprise AI platform to employees across Samsung's Device Experience division worldwide, including in Korea. The two companies are calling it their largest enterprise agentic AI deployment in the country so far, built on a dedicated tenant for data sovereignty, with simple no-code agent building available now and more autonomous agents planned later. It is a reminder that the fiercest competition for enterprise AI deployment at scale is increasingly being fought out in Asia's biggest electronics and manufacturing conglomerates, not just in Silicon Valley.
Now, over to A.I. and tech, where the story with the most staying power this week is a warning letter rather than a launch. More than two hundred AI researchers and economists, including sixteen Nobel laureates, have signed a Stanford-organised statement called We Must Act Now, urging governments to build safety nets and labour policy for an economic shift its authors compare to the Industrial Revolution, only much faster. Signatories include Google's Jeff Dean, Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark and OpenAI's Noam Brown, and the core argument is blunt: steam, electricity and computers each gave societies decades to adjust, but AI may only give the world a few years. The letter is heavy on signatories and light on specifics, which is exactly the point critics will make, but getting rival labs' own people to agree publicly on the scale of the problem is not nothing.
In security news with a very now flavour, researchers have unveiled a technique called GhostCommit that hides prompt injection instructions inside an image pushed to a code repository, designed to fool AI coding agents into leaking secrets. When a coding agent later reads that image, it follows hidden instructions to copy environment files and upload their contents byte by byte disguised as harmless numbers. In testing, the researchers found that pull request review agents tended to skip over images entirely, letting the poisoned commit sail through untouched, and that both Cursor and Antigravity followed the hidden instructions under certain models. Encouragingly, Opus running inside Claude Code spotted the social engineering attempt and refused to comply, a useful data point as coding agents get wired ever more deeply into everyday developer workflows.
On the product side, Apple has pushed out the first public beta of iOS twenty seven, and the headline feature is a rebuilt Siri that can hold an ongoing conversation, understand what is on your screen, take actions inside apps and answer much broader questions than before. It will run on any iPhone currently on iOS twenty six, though the full Apple Intelligence features need an iPhone fifteen Pro or newer. Quietly, in the same week, Apple's own on-device speech recognition system was benchmarked against OpenAI's Whisper for the first time and came out clearly ahead on accuracy while using a fraction of the compute, suggesting Apple's hardware advantage in everyday AI features is more real than the company's public image around AI usually gets credit for.
Now, over to startups and venture, where Sifted's reporting today is really a story about money quietly leaving one sector and piling into others. Generalist European venture funds have cut their average fintech portfolio share by almost two thirds since twenty twenty one, a retreat driven by the arrival of AI as the new default excitement and by higher interest rates making fintech's slower, more regulated growth look a lot less attractive by comparison. Investors interviewed for the piece had blunt advice for founders navigating the drought: keep existing backers close and ask them for brutally honest feedback rather than burning months chasing a growth round that was never really there, and build contingency plans through family offices or debt rather than assuming the next check is coming.
Defence technology, by contrast, is having no trouble attracting capital. The German firm Helsing has raised one point eight billion dollars backed by Goldman Sachs and Lightspeed, one of the larger rounds in European tech so far this year and further confirmation that European investors and governments alike are treating defence and dual-use technology as a durable category rather than a wartime blip. In the same roundup, Anthropic recruited Monzo cofounder Tom Blomfield to work on its AI compute team, and savings app Moneybox was crowned one of Europe's newest unicorns.
And in legal tech, Harvey, the eleven billion dollar AI startup for lawyers, says it plans to double its European headcount and open new offices, with its EMEA boss telling Sifted that Europe could soon drive up to a third of the company's global growth. Harvey is actively hunting acquisitions to fill product gaps or bring in specialist talent, and is pushing beyond law into private equity, insurance and other knowledge-heavy industries, even as Swedish rival Legora pursues its own aggressive hiring and dealmaking. With OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Cursor all expanding their European footprints too, the real test for Europe's AI-native legal and professional services startups is whether they can keep growing organically before better-funded American rivals simply buy their way into the market.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics, where nuclear tension is very much back on the agenda. President Trump said on Monday that the United States would strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain facility and warned that Washington would keep hitting the country hard, while new satellite imagery obtained by CNN and analysed alongside the Institute for Science and International Security suggests Iran may already be attempting to rebuild suspected nuclear sites. It is a sharp reminder that, whatever else is dominating headlines, the underlying Iran nuclear file never really closed.
Further east, a new analysis from the Stimson Center argues that Pakistan's acquisition of the Hangor submarine signals three things at once: deepening cooperation between China and Pakistan, an Islamabad push towards a submarine-launched nuclear cruise missile to strengthen its second-strike capability, and intensifying maritime competition with India. Coming in the same week that North Korea condemned the recent NATO summit and insisted its own weapons programme is a sovereign right rather than a threat, it underlines how much of the world's nuclear posturing this year is happening in Asia rather than Europe, even when Europe dominates the headlines.
And speaking of Europe, French president Emmanuel Macron became the first major Western leader to visit Damascus since the fall of the Assad regime, signing memoranda on healthcare and transport while pushing to reestablish French influence and secure a share of Syria's reconstruction contracts, a trip overshadowed by two unclaimed bomb blasts near his hotel. Back home days later, Macron hosted roughly twenty five leaders from the so-called Coalition of the Willing to discuss further support for Ukraine, even as new reporting showed the European Union had bought a record amount of liquefied natural gas from Russia's own Arctic export terminal in the first half of this year alone, a gap between solidarity rhetoric and energy practice that is exactly the kind of detail worth having ready for the next conversation about European resolve.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, where the idea worth stealing this week is about deciding what to actually measure. The writer Amanda Natividad argues that most marketing metrics do not deserve a standing weekly meeting, because the real test of a number is not how interesting it looks on a dashboard but whether it would ever change a decision you are about to make. In her telling, one podcast agency founder ignores individual open rates and click counts almost entirely and watches only whether qualified leads are turning into the customers the business actually needs, freeing her team to experiment with channels rather than optimising vanity metrics that were never going to move anything.
And Skift's meetings desk reported on new research from the U.S. Travel Association that should worry anyone pitching a corporate event this year: the usual language of getting inspired and making connections, which is how most face-to-face gatherings sell themselves to attendees, is failing to persuade the executives who actually approve the budget. The practical takeaway for planners is to stop leading with inspiration and start leading with the harder business case, tying an event's cost directly to measurable outcomes, since that is the argument that is actually landing with the people holding the purse strings.
Finally, one interesting thing to take you into the day. The newsletter Why Is This Interesting has a lovely piece this week on why some of the best footballers on the pitch look like they are moving in slow motion. French winger Michael Olise, playing in this week's World Cup semi-final, reads the game with his brain before his legs ever move, anticipating a pass or a run so early that defenders closing at full pace never quite arrive in time; his workload numbers are as high as anyone's, so the stillness people see is really just anticipation dressed up as calm. Lionel Messi achieves the same visual effect a completely different way, covering less ground per ninety minutes than almost any other outfield player at this tournament while still leading it in goals, because his teammates run so he does not have to. Both are proof that speed of thought beats speed of motion, a line that applies rather well beyond football too.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and I'll see you back here tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Tuesday, 14 July
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized. It's Tuesday, the fourteenth of July, and today we've got six sections lined up: Japan and Asia-Pacific, A.I. and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community, events and marketing, and one interesting thing to close us out. Let's get into it.
Starting with Japan and Asia-Pacific. New Delhi's Great Nicobar Project is being read by regional watchers as India's formal arrival as an Indian Ocean power, a signal that the archipelago at the mouth of the Malacca Strait is becoming a genuine strategic asset rather than a remote outpost, as India builds out infrastructure that lets it project influence along one of the world's busiest shipping corridors. The move sits alongside a steady run of Indian Ocean activity from rival and allied navies alike, and it is the kind of quiet infrastructure story that tends to matter far more in five years than it does the week it is announced.
Over in Seoul, CSIS convened its Capital Cable series this week to take stock of one year of the Lee Jae Myung administration, weighing how the government has handled its early foreign policy and economic choices against the expectations it set on taking office. A year in is normally when a government's actual priorities, as opposed to its campaign promises, become visible, and this is exactly the kind of stocktaking that is worth watching for anyone tracking how Seoul balances its relationships with Washington and Beijing.
And closer to home for Japanese founders, the research firm SPEEDA, part of Uzabase, is bringing together three corporate innovation leads this month, from JGC Holdings, Keio Corporation and Mitsubishi Materials, to dig into a problem familiar to anyone who has tried to launch a new business inside a large company: the original plan almost never survives contact with customers, markets and internal politics unchanged. Their shared argument is that the real skill large firms need is not the ability to execute a fixed vision, but the organisational muscle to keep exploring and revising judgment as assumptions shift, whether that means building a corporate venture arm, as Keio has done, or systematically connecting new technology to market need, as Mitsubishi Materials has tried to do. It is a useful reminder that Japan's biggest companies are still actively wrestling with how to make internal entrepreneurship work, rather than treating it as solved.
Now, over to A.I. and tech, where the week's biggest story is a lawsuit rather than a launch. Apple has sued OpenAI, accusing it of stealing confidential trade secrets and unreleased hardware information through former Apple employees, one of whom allegedly kept access to Apple's internal network after leaving, using a previously unknown authentication flaw and a colleague's still-active credentials to get back in. Apple is seeking damages, the destruction of any misused material, and changes to OpenAI's future hardware if Apple's technology shows up in it. The commentary site The Diff points out that when a company wants to prove theft without revealing exactly what was taken, the trick is to make the circumstantial picture of bad behaviour as damning as possible, and Apple's filing does precisely that. It is an awkward moment for a relationship that still includes OpenAI powering parts of Apple Intelligence, even as the two increasingly compete on hardware.
Elsewhere in AI products this week, Figma acquired the team behind Bud, a vibe-coding and AI agent platform, folding it into its own push toward app-building tools, while Meta pulled its Muse image AI feature from Instagram and WhatsApp just three days after launch, after the tool let users generate images from any public account by default and drew a swift backlash from Hollywood talent agencies and performers.
And on the more reflective side, the newsletter Every argues that as AI agents take over the actual writing of code, the valuable human work left is polish: opening the finished feature yourself, using it as a real user would, and telling the agent what feels off until it doesn't. A model doesn't know what "good" means for your product and your users sitting in front of it, so that final layer of taste and judgment is becoming the part of software work that agents can't yet do for you. Via Every.
Now, over to startups and venture, where the week's best story is also its briefest. Sifted reported that the AI scientist Yann LeCun was launching a new fund, Extelligence Invest, backed by sources close to the deal and confirmed by LeCun's own spokesperson before publication. Within eight hours of that story going live, the fund's website had been taken down, LeCun's team said he had withdrawn over what they called existing exclusive relationships with other funds, and Extelligence itself announced it was shutting down the entire launch. By Saturday the website was back up, scrubbed of any names at all. It's a reminder of just how fast reputational plumbing can unwind once one thread gets pulled in public.
Underneath the drama, TLDR's founders newsletter carried a sharper structural point this week: foundation models, for all the capital and brilliance behind them, don't have a durable business model of their own, because every new release makes the last one obsolete, and enterprises are increasingly buying intelligence the way they buy electricity, as an interchangeable commodity. The flip side, the newsletter argues, is that the biggest financial winners from AI won't be AI companies at all, but low-margin businesses that finally have a cheap way to attack the coordination costs that have kept them structurally unprofitable for decades.
And in a smaller but telling consolidation move, Booking Holdings is forming a new business-to-business unit that brings Booking.com, Agoda and Priceline together to power travel offerings for other companies, putting Agoda's chief executive in charge of an effort to catch up with Expedia's already sizeable B2B arm, which grew three times faster last quarter than its consumer business. Via Skift.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics, where CSIS hosted a panel this week on the two Section 301 investigations the US Trade Representative is running into forced labour and industrial overcapacity, with China a central target in both. Panellists compared the current probe to the 2017 to 2018 investigation into Chinese intellectual property theft, and the framing question running through it was whether Washington's legal, economic and diplomatic toolkit is any better suited this time to managing a trade relationship that keeps generating fresh points of friction.
And CSIS's Futures Lab published a striking piece of geographic analysis on Russia's missile and drone campaign in Ukraine, mapping oblast-level damage reports from 2023 through early this year to show how Moscow is concentrating strikes on frontline and southern regions, industrial and energy infrastructure, ports and major cities. The pattern suggests a deliberate coercive logic: using long-range firepower not just for battlefield effect but to strain Ukraine's ability to repair, govern and negotiate, with cheap Shahed-type drones letting Russia sustain a far higher tempo of attacks than precision missiles alone would allow.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, where two ideas are worth stealing this week rather than just noting. The facilitator Priya Parker argues that a single well-run gathering, whether a family meeting, a celebration or an offsite, works because it gives people connection instead of performance: focus on a small group of the right people rather than a large group of the wrong ones, and let meaning and fun sit alongside each other rather than treating them as competing goals.
And the CMX community newsletter closed out its webinar series with a sharper version of the same point aimed at workplaces. One guest speaker's take was that engagement metrics aren't the outcome of community work, they're just the fuel, and that reporting pipeline influence and retention instead of registrations and badges is what actually gets leadership to invest. Another argued that community managers aren't generalists who failed to specialise, they're the only people in a company who sit in the middle of marketing's story, product's story and everyone else's, and that vantage point is a genuine strength rather than a lack of focus. Via CMX.
Finally, one interesting thing to take you into the day. The economist Tyler Cowen gave a talk at DeepMind this month reflecting on what he calls an exhaustion of meaning rather than a shortage of it. His argument is that as models improve at a relentless pace, the problem for many people won't be finding purpose, it will be coping with how much purpose, stimulation and pressure to keep up a fast-moving world now generates, especially for anyone young enough to fear falling behind if they don't jump on each new wave immediately. He points to his own working life as evidence: he says he is busier now because of AI, not despite it, driven by a wage gradient that rewards engaging with each new model the moment it appears. The eventual leisure dividend from all this technology may well arrive, he suggests, but probably on a much longer horizon than the exhaustion that comes first.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and I'll see you back here tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Monday, 13 July
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized. It's Monday, the thirteenth of July, and today we've got six sections lined up: Japan and Asia-Pacific, A.I. and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community, events and marketing, and one interesting thing to close us out. Let's get into it.
Starting with Japan and Asia-Pacific. It was a quiet morning for regional headlines, but one number from CSIS is worth sitting with: South Korea's trade surplus with China has collapsed over the past decade, from around ninety nine point seven billion dollars in twenty eighteen down to just nineteen point six billion dollars last year, as Chinese firms increasingly out-compete Korean exporters across electronics, electric vehicles, batteries and petrochemicals. A CSIS analysis this week frames that slide as a genuine fork in the road for Seoul: keep trying to out-export a rival that is closing the technology gap, or pivot toward becoming what the piece calls an ecosystem power, building the platforms, standards and artificial intelligence infrastructure that other economies plug into, rather than just the goods they sell them. It is a choice with obvious echoes for Japan's own export-led model, which has spent decades leaning on precisely the kind of manufacturing scale that China is now matching or beating on cost, and it is worth watching as a bellwether for how the wider region, Tokyo included, responds to China's continuing manufacturing advance. The underlying question for both economies is essentially the same one facing exporters right across the Asia-Pacific: whether the old formula of out-producing everyone else at a lower price still works once a rival with China's scale decides to compete on the same terms, or whether the more durable advantage now lies further up the value chain, in the standards, software and data that sit around the hardware rather than the hardware itself. Via CSIS.
Now, over to A.I. and tech, where the week's story was less about one blockbuster launch and more about the ground shifting under the existing model war, both for the machines and for the people using them.
Start with the people. The second annual Tech Worker Sentiment Survey, run by longtime research leader Noam Segal alongside Lenny's Newsletter, found the industry splitting almost exactly in half: one half of workers thriving alongside artificial intelligence, the other shaken by it, with four distinct emotional groups emerging from the data, ranging from the energised to the outright resentful. Burnout has jumped sharply over the past year, and, tellingly, the survey's authors found the number one fear among tech workers right now is not losing a job to artificial intelligence outright, it is something closer to the erosion of meaning, status and support at work, with line managers emerging as the single biggest lever for employee wellbeing. Via Lenny's Newsletter.
On the model side, Grok four point five arrived this week as the first product of a formal collaboration between SpaceXAI and the coding tool Cursor, trained in part on real coding-tool interaction data. Early internal testing at the newsletter Every put it roughly level with Anthropic's Opus four point eight on tricky multi-step assignments, while running faster and considerably cheaper, at around two dollars per million input tokens against Opus's five, and with none of Claude's more familiar writing tics, if its own habit of short, blunt sentences instead. It is not necessarily a reason to switch your daily coding assistant, but for long jobs where speed and price matter more than the very top of the quality curve, it has already earned a slot in some workflows.
Meanwhile, Every's own team has quietly settled on OpenAI's GPT five point six, nicknamed Sol, as its default daily driver, prized less for raw brilliance than for being fast, easy to steer and reliable across coding, writing, research and spreadsheets, with the pricier Fable model reserved for the biggest, least-defined assignments. The clearest sign of how seriously that shift is being taken: the team has open-sourced a tool called Tend, a free prompt and workflow for letting a model run an entire loop of knowledge work largely on its own, gathering information, proposing decisions and carrying out the ones a human approves, while the person "tends" the loop rather than doing each step by hand.
And underneath all of it, a broader mood shift: as the big labs pull back the generous subsidies that made frontier models cheap to hammer with tokens, the conversation inside engineering and product teams is moving from what Every calls tokenmaxxing, bragging about how many tokens a workflow burns, to efficiencymaxxing, competing instead on how much useful output you can squeeze from a fixed budget, with "revenue per million tokens" emerging as an early candidate for the metric that actually matters. Via Every.
Now, over to startups and venture, where the sharpest piece of the week was less about a single deal than about the industry's own self-doubt. A long essay from The VC Corner traced venture capital's evolution from a handful of wealthy friends taking handshake bets on nineteen-fifties San Francisco semiconductor engineers, through the built-out, tens-of-billions-under-management industry it is today, to argue that the model itself is now under real strain. Returns have become harder to predict, exit timelines keep stretching, and portfolio companies are staying private for far longer than the traditional ten-year fund cycle was ever designed to absorb, prompting what the piece calls a civil war inside the asset class over how much operational hand-holding, rather than just capital, a fund now needs to offer founders to stay competitive. The essay traces that pressure all the way back to the industry's origins as a cottage business of outsiders willing to back ideas that sounded like science fiction, and argues the funds most likely to come out ahead now are the ones rediscovering that original willingness to sit with genuine uncertainty, rather than the ones simply managing an ever-larger pool of capital more cautiously. It is a useful reminder, in a week without a headline mega-round, that the plumbing behind the funding announcements is quietly being rebuilt under pressure. Via The VC Corner.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics, where CSIS's regular numbers round-up doubled as a snapshot of where hard power and hard resources are both heading. The White House's budget request for the twenty twenty seven fiscal year would push total defence spending to around four point six percent of gross domestic product, a notable increase but still, by CSIS's own reckoning, short of what counts as a genuine wartime footing. That matters because Russia is now firing more than five thousand drones a month into Ukraine, leaning on cheap Shahed-type craft precisely because their low cost lets Moscow launch far bigger, more frequent salvos than missiles alone would allow, a pattern of coercion by volume rather than precision. Underneath both numbers sits a resource story: China still controls roughly sixty percent of the world's primary aluminium production, some forty three million tonnes a year, while the United States imports around eighty two percent of its own primary supply, which is why mining group Alcoa's move to deepen a bet on South African aluminium is being read in Washington as a small but deliberate step toward keeping a strategic metal in allied hands. Via CSIS.
Closer to home, in Washington, the Trump administration is pushing ahead with a rewrite of the federal government's core grantmaking regulation, the kind of rule that sounds mundane but effectively decides how America's decentralised, historically successful system of science funding actually works in practice. The pushback has been unusually blunt and unusually bipartisan: the American Association for the Advancement of Science has called it a brazen power grab by the Office of Management and Budget that would leave future cures and discoveries hostage to the "scientific sensibilities" of a single budget analyst, while commentators from The Dispatch on the right to Noah Smith and Dan Drezner on the centre-left warn the rule would hand political appointees sweeping discretion to cancel or redirect funding for ideological reasons, with little recourse for researchers caught in the middle. Via Marginal Revolution.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, where this week's idea worth stealing is a small structural one. The Do Lectures' weekly newsletter leads every single edition with a segment called This Week's Changemaker, handing the very top slot to one small business or maker doing something quietly hard, before any of the week's other links or recommendations. It is a simple habit any community newsletter or events programme could copy without much extra effort: pick one person or one project each week and give them first billing, rather than burying individual stories inside one long, undifferentiated list. Via The Do Lectures.
Finally, one interesting thing to take you into the week ahead. New research on both sides of the Atlantic suggests something odd is happening to how young people talk about their own mental health. The share of young Britons and Americans who say they have a mental illness has climbed sharply over the past fifteen years, but the share who say a mental health problem actually limits their day-to-day functioning has barely moved at all. When people are asked whether ordinary mood swings, occasional worry, frustration, a wobble in confidence, should count as mental illness, more than half of young Americans now say yes, up from roughly a fifth fifteen years ago, while older people's answers have not shifted in the same period. It looks less like a sudden epidemic of illness than a generational change in vocabulary, in what people now consider worth naming out loud. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and I'll see you back here tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Sunday, 12 July
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized, your week in review for the week of the sixth of July. I'm your host, and today we've got six sections lined up: Japan and Asia-Pacific, A.I. and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community, events and marketing, and one interesting thing to close us out. Let's get into it.
Starting, as always, with Japan and Asia-Pacific. The week's throughline here was a quiet operational shift rather than a loud headline: how much of the region's competitive edge, in manufacturing and in security, is being redrawn by artificial intelligence and by Washington's retreat from old certainties.
First, a story from the shop floor. A Japanese business newsletter this week looked at what's actually happening inside factories as artificial intelligence spreads through manufacturing. Fully automated, A.I.-run factories are due to come online in Germany later this year, but surveys of Japanese manufacturing sites suggest genuine, in-production use of A.I. still sits at only around one in ten plants. The piece argues that's not simply Japan lagging behind. It's a sign that the old markers of industrial strength, the size of your equipment, your production volume, the depth of your veteran workforce's know-how, are starting to matter less than a newer one: how much operational data a company actually controls. As artificial intelligence takes over more of the routine judgement calls on a factory floor, that data may end up being the last thing standing between a competitive plant and an obsolete one, and Japanese manufacturers who have spent decades optimising for scale are now having to relearn what their real advantage is. Via Speeda A.I. News.
Second, the South China Sea remains stubbornly unresolved. It's now ten years since an international tribunal found the vast majority of China's claims there unlawful, and the risk of conflict has not eased. A CSIS podcast this week brought together two China watchers, including the author of a recent book on America's century in the South China Sea, to unpack why Beijing continues to press its claims over a scattering of rocks and reefs, what has and hasn't worked in its strategy, and why the waterway remains one of the sharpest flashpoints in the US-China relationship. The conversation lands just as CSIS wraps its sixteenth annual South China Sea conference, now available to watch back in full, and just as the think tank's Southeast Asia programme sent out a late agenda change ahead of that same gathering, a small sign of how fluid the diplomatic choreography around the region still is. Via CSIS.
And rounding out the region, CSIS is hosting a congressional perspective on the Indo-Pacific later this month, with Senator Tammy Duckworth addressing strategic competition, alliances and the future of American engagement, alongside a separate CSIS briefing this week on India's economic outlook and investment risks for 2026, and a running weekly roundup out of CSIS tracking state-level policy reform across the Indo-Pacific, from electricity grid codes to trade rules, country by country. Together they're a reminder that Washington's Indo-Pacific strategy is still, three and a half years into this decade, more a work in progress than a settled doctrine, and that India increasingly sits at the centre of how that strategy gets built, both as a security partner and as the biggest single economy still deciding how closely to align itself with Washington versus keeping its options open. Via CSIS.
Now, over to A.I. and tech, which had one of its busiest weeks in months, on both the product and the security side. Where the week landed: a fresh round of flagship model launches, a genuinely interesting research result out of Anthropic, an uncomfortable string of agent-security disclosures, and mounting evidence that the hardware and the humans underneath this boom are both starting to strain.
The headline act was OpenAI's release of its GPT five point six family, three tiers named Sol, Terra and Luna, with Sol as the flagship, pitched as leading on intelligence and efficiency for coding, cybersecurity and scientific work. It landed the same week SpaceXAI released Grok four point five, which the company says was trained alongside Cursor and is aimed squarely at coding and agentic tasks, and the same week Meta pushed out Muse Image, its first in-house A.I. image model, now powering tools across the Meta A.I. app, Instagram and WhatsApp. The model wars, in other words, did not pause for the weekend, and they're increasingly geopolitical too: Alibaba has reportedly told staff to stop using Claude Code altogether, classifying it as high-risk software and pushing employees toward its own homegrown coding tool instead, a small but pointed sign that the frontier A.I. stack is being treated as a matter of national technology sovereignty, not just vendor choice. Via TLDR, the Rundown and This Week in Startups.
Anthropic had its own moment. New research from the company describes something it's calling J-space: internal neural patterns inside Claude that appear to play a distinct, previously unrecognised role in how the model reasons. In the same week, Anthropic also expanded Claude Cowork, its general knowledge-work agent, from a desktop-only tool to web and mobile, currently in beta for its highest tier of subscribers. Together, the two stories point the same direction: frontier labs are spending as much energy understanding what's happening inside their models as they are shipping new ones. Via TLDR and the Rundown.
The security side of that same story was less flattering. Researchers this week showed they could trick GitHub's own agentic workflow into reading private repository files and posting their contents back as a public comment, using little more than a crafted issue and the word additionally to slip past its guardrails. A near-identical flaw in Google's Dialogflow let anyone with a modest permission level hijack chat sessions across an entire project. And security firm Sysdig documented what's being called the first largely autonomous ransomware attack, an A.I. agent that breached a server, pivoted into a database, encrypted more than one thousand three hundred records and wrote its own ransom note, though a human was still needed to set it in motion. Read together, it's a reminder that the same agentic capabilities being celebrated on the product side of this industry are being probed just as hard from the other direction. Via TLDR Information Security.
Meanwhile, the physical and human costs of all this abundance came into sharper focus. The price of computer memory has roughly tripled in six months, driven by the same data centre boom powering the A.I. build-out, and chipmakers are redirecting supply toward server memory, meaning anyone buying a phone, laptop or games console this year will likely feel it too; Nvidia's own next rack-scale system, Kyber, has reportedly slipped by more than a year to 2028, a sign even the biggest players are hitting real physical bottlenecks. Inside engineering teams, the strain looks different but points the same way: a survey this week found burnout among tech workers has climbed to fifty five point seven percent, up from forty four point seven percent a year ago, even as a separate analysis found power users now writing ten times as many lines of code as the median engineer, most A.I. coding spend going on input tokens rather than output, and nearly half of all A.I.-generated code changes now being accepted without manual review, against a backdrop of thirty five actively maintained command-line coding agents now competing for developers' attention. Read together, it's a profession being reshaped faster than its people, or its supply chains, have managed to settle. Via The Generalist, Lenny's Newsletter, The Pragmatic Engineer and TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture, where the week landed on a familiar split: eye-watering valuations at the frontier, and a very different, quieter kind of momentum building underneath at the bootstrapped end of the market.
The biggest number of the week belonged to Lovable, the European vibe-coding darling, which is reportedly in talks to raise three hundred million dollars at a valuation of thirteen point two billion dollars, roughly double the six point six billion dollar valuation it carried after its December funding round. If it closes, it will be one of the fastest re-ratings European tech has seen this year. Via Sifted and TLDR.
Fintech infrastructure also stirred on both sides of the Atlantic. Plaid has opened preliminary talks with investment banks about a possible public listing, the clearest signal yet that the long-dormant fintech IPO window may finally be creaking back open, while British core-banking software maker Thought Machine confirmed it has crossed one hundred million dollars in annual recurring revenue and is weighing its own path toward an eventual listing, a milestone that took the company the better part of a decade to reach and underlines how much longer the patient, infrastructure end of fintech takes to compound compared with the consumer apps built on top of it. Via TLDR and Sifted.
And in a smaller but telling story, Yann LeCun, the veteran A.I. researcher recently departed from Meta, is said to be in talks with limited partners about launching his own venture capital firm, the latest sign that star researchers are increasingly choosing to become allocators of capital rather than staying inside the big labs, a shift echoed by a widely shared essay this week profiling a low-profile investor once described as the best in the business that almost nobody outside Silicon Valley has heard of. Via Sifted and The VC Corner.
Underneath the big rounds, the solo and bootstrapped end of the market kept humming along too. Indie Hackers' weekly roundup this week featured a solo founder now clearing one hundred and twenty five thousand dollars a month in recurring revenue without any outside funding, alongside a running theme of founders leaning on a handful of vibe-coding tools to ship products with barely any traditional engineering headcount at all, a reminder that the same A.I. tooling reshaping big engineering teams is also quietly lowering the bar for one-person companies. Via Indie Hackers.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics, where the week landed on two familiar themes: Washington quietly hardening its trade posture toward its own neighbours as much as toward China, and Moscow continuing to test Europe's edges by whatever means are cheapest, whether that's disinformation, hacking or simply patience.
Trade policy delivered the week's clearest signal: the first of July deadline for reviewing the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement came and went with Washington declining to renew it as originally structured, leaving the future of North America's central trade pact genuinely uncertain for the first time since it was signed. A CSIS discussion this week walked through what that decision means for supply chains and diplomacy across the continent. Separately, the US Trade Representative's office is pressing ahead with two Section 301 investigations into whether forced labour and industrial overcapacity elsewhere, China chief among the countries named, are harming American trade interests. A CSIS panel convening next week, featuring voices from the Asia Society, the Peterson Institute and the Middlebury Institute, will compare the case directly to the 2017 intellectual property investigation that reshaped US-China trade relations for years afterward. Via CSIS.
And in Europe, Russia's shadow war rolled on across two very different fronts. In Moldova, the country's push for European Union accession is increasingly being read not as a routine enlargement file but as a test of whether Europe can actually harden a vulnerable young democracy against Russian hybrid interference on its eastern border. At almost the same moment, Britain confirmed that several government officials' email accounts had been compromised through the FortiBleed vulnerability, with the stolen credentials put up for sale on the dark web for around sixty thousand dollars; investigators say the attackers appear to be Russian-speaking, though not obviously state directed. Two different theatres, the same underlying pressure Moscow continues to apply on Europe's edges. Via Geopoliticalmonitor and TLDR.
A third thread worth flagging: the resource competition underneath all of this is intensifying too. Saudi Arabia's Manara Minerals spin-off was highlighted this week as a case study in how sovereign wealth is shifting from passive stakes in mining companies to direct control over the processing stage of critical minerals supply chains, the same minerals that underpin everything from electric vehicles to the chips powering this week's A.I. announcements. Via Geopoliticalmonitor.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, where the idea worth stealing this week is about grabbing attention honestly rather than loudly.
The Do Lectures, the long-running ideas and storytelling event, is previewing its next gathering under the theme New Rules of Attention, arguing that in a landscape of infinite scroll, the events and talks that cut through are the ones built around a single, well-earned idea rather than a crowded agenda. It's a useful discipline for anyone planning a community gathering of their own: fewer speakers, harder editing, one thing people actually remember. Via The Do Lectures.
In a similar vein, facilitator and author Priya Parker used this week's newsletter to make the case that the single most powerful tool for shaping any group gathering, a dinner, a meeting, a conference, is deceptively simple: naming a specific, disputed purpose for the room out loud before it starts, rather than defaulting to a vague agenda everyone nods along to. It's a small habit that's easy to steal for the next team offsite or community meet-up. Via Priya Parker.
There was also a small but instructive case study in restarting from scratch. David Spinks, one of the best-known voices in community building, used this week to launch a brand new newsletter under his own name after years building out other people's platforms, a reminder that even established operators periodically need to tear up the format and reintroduce themselves plainly rather than lean on an old audience out of habit. Via David Spinks.
And on the more literal end of grabbing attention, Marketing Brew flagged Miller Lite's stunt of the week: floating a barge loaded with beer into Miami for the Fourth of July, a reminder that in a summer crowded with brand noise, a single well-timed physical stunt can still out-perform a much bigger paid media budget. Via Marketing Brew.
Finally, one interesting thing to take you into the week ahead.
Roughly eight percent of the land in America's major coastal cities, think Boston, Manhattan, San Francisco, was underwater as recently as the eighteen nineties and has since been filled in and built on. For most of American history, land reclamation was routine engineering, not a controversial idea. Then, around the middle of the last century, the practice all but stopped, even as those same cities ran short of buildable land and housing costs climbed. The essay behind this week's pick argues the halt was driven less by engineering limits than by a shift in how Americans came to see the coastline itself, from a resource to be shaped into something closer to sacred ground, protected by exactly the kind of environmental review process that now makes filling in even a modest stretch of shoreline practically unthinkable. It's a neat companion piece to everything else this week's episode has covered: a reminder that the biggest constraints on growth, in old industries as much as new ones, are as often cultural as they are technical. Via Works in Progress.
That's your week in review. Thanks for listening, and I'll see you back here tomorrow for the next episode of Byte-sized.

item.title: Byte-sized — Saturday, 11 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Saturday, the eleventh of July, and here are six sections to get you up to speed: Japan and Asia Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community and marketing, and one interesting thing to close.
In Japan, a note from Speeda's AI News team argues that artificial intelligence is starting to quietly reshuffle what actually makes a factory strong. A fully AI driven factory is due to go live in Germany later this year, yet by contrast only around one in ten Japanese manufacturing sites currently run AI in full production use rather than as a pilot. The team's argument is that this isn't simply Japan lagging on AI adoption, it's a sign that the old measures of factory strength, plant size, output volume, decades of shop floor expertise, are starting to matter less than which company actually holds the richest stream of on site data. As AI takes over more of the routine judgement calls on a factory floor, the piece argues, what's left as a genuine competitive edge is increasingly about data, not machinery. Via Speeda Intelligence.
Staying with AI policy across the region, CSIS's monthly Pac Tech roundup flags a burst of new rules from Beijing and Delhi. China has issued fresh guidelines standardising how AI agents are built and graded, alongside a plan to more tightly integrate AI computing with clean energy supply, targeting a big expansion of clean power for AI data centres by twenty thirty. China has also published a national grading system for how intelligent everyday devices, from smart glasses to car cockpits, are allowed to claim to be. India, meanwhile, has launched a National AI Doctors Mission to train medical professionals across the country in AI applications, clinical practice and the ethical use of digital healthcare tools. Via CSIS.
And there's a reminder of how central this region now is to the AI economy in the International Monetary Fund's latest World Economic Outlook. Even as the fund only trimmed its twenty twenty six global growth forecast slightly, to three percent, despite the Iran war rattling oil markets, it flagged outsized growth surprises for the world's top four AI linked hardware exporters, Taiwan, South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia, underlining how much of the current AI boom is being built, quite literally, in Asian factories and fabs. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to AI and tech.
OpenAI has now actually released its GPT five point six family, after days of anticipation. The line-up has three tiers: Sol, the flagship model leading on intelligence and efficiency for coding, cybersecurity and science work; Terra, a cheaper mid tier model roughly matching the current GPT five point five at half the price; and Luna, the fastest and cheapest option of the three, aimed at high volume everyday tasks. Early hands on impressions, including from the team at Every, describe Sol as fast and easy to steer, though they say Anthropic's Fable model still gets the assignments they want to hand off completely. Via TLDR, The Rundown and Every.
Not to be outdone, SpaceXAI has launched Grok four point five, which it's pitching as its strongest model yet for coding, agentic tasks and general knowledge work, saying it was trained alongside Cursor and that early benchmarks put it roughly level with Anthropic's Opus four point eight and OpenAI's GPT five point five. Via TLDR.
On the security side, npm has released version twelve with install scripts, git dependencies and installs from remote URLs all switched off by default, forcing developers to explicitly approve anything that behaves that way, a direct response to the wave of supply chain attacks that have hit the open source ecosystem this year, including well over a hundred exploits published against popular packages in recent months. Via TLDR.
And a data dump from Cursor, relayed by the Pragmatic Engineer, gives a rare look at how AI coding tools are actually being used inside companies. Power users are writing ten times as many lines of code as the median developer, most AI spending is going on input tokens rather than output, and almost half of AI generated code changes are now being accepted without a manual review, a figure that raises real questions about how much scrutiny AI written code is actually getting. Via The Pragmatic Engineer.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Yann LeCun, who left Meta earlier this year to found the AI lab AMI Labs, is reportedly now in talks with limited partners about launching a separate venture capital firm of his own, a sign of how many star AI researchers are turning into fund managers as well as founders this year. Via Sifted.
Sifted's rundown of the first half of twenty twenty six's biggest new venture funds lands alongside news that European quantum sensing startup QuantumDiamonds has closed a ninety one million euro round, another sign of investors piling into deep tech even as the wider funding market stays choosy about everything else. Via Sifted.
And a widely shared piece is pushing back hard on the idea that AI is gutting the job market. Citing Atlanta Fed survey data, it points out that over ninety percent of American firms that adopted AI in the past three years reported no change at all in headcount, and argues the underlying assumption, that there's a fixed amount of work to go around, has failed to hold up against every previous wave of labour saving technology for two hundred years. The real shift, it argues, isn't fewer jobs, it's companies quietly redesigning who does what, which makes hiring the right people into the right roles harder, not easier. Via The VC Corner.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
China has carried out its first ever long range submarine launched ballistic missile test, firing a nuclear capable missile roughly seven thousand three hundred kilometres across the Pacific to a splashdown near Tuvalu, Nauru and Kiribati, its first announced submarine launch since nineteen eighty eight. Unlike China's previous short coastal tests, a shot of this range sends a clear message to Washington that the submarine leg of its nuclear arsenal can now credibly reach the US mainland, even as Beijing publicly urged the world not to read too much into it. Via International Intrigue.
That test landed the same week as the IMF's new World Economic Outlook, which held its twenty twenty six global growth forecast at close to three percent despite the Iran war's shock to oil markets, helped in part by China's large but opaque oil reserves cushioning the blow. It flagged a much less comfortable story on prices though: a revised inflation forecast of four point seven percent that, if it holds, would mark the first real break in the world's post twenty twenty two disinflation trend, driven by higher and more volatile energy, food and fertiliser costs. Via International Intrigue.
And in Europe, Moldova's path toward European Union membership is increasingly being treated as a test case for the whole bloc, as Chisinau tries to hold its democracy together against a sustained Russian hybrid war campaign of disinformation and interference aimed at derailing accession. How Brussels handles Moldova, the argument goes, will say a lot about whether the EU can actually protect the vulnerable democracies on its eastern edge, rather than just talk about doing so. Via Geopolitical Monitor.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Here's an idea worth stealing if you want earned attention rather than paid reach. Miller Lite literally sent a barge loaded with beer to Miami this week, a stunt built for social sharing and local news pickup rather than a conventional ad buy, betting that a strange, photographable spectacle travels further than the same budget spent on banners. Via Marketing Brew.
And for community builders, Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering, offers a simpler takeaway worth stealing: before you redesign your next dinner, meeting or event, just start noticing. Watch how people already behave at the gatherings you're already part of, and ask what the group actually needs, what's working, and what's quietly missing, because that habit of paying attention does more for the quality of a gathering than a good playlist or an expensive cheese board ever will. Via Priya Parker.
Now, over to one interesting thing to leave you with.
A links roundup from Works in Progress catches you up on how fast biology is moving this year: a synthetic cell built entirely through chemistry rather than biological machinery, a new laser based electron microscopy technique giving sharper images of proteins than ever before, the first base edited human embryo, and early progress toward lab grown eggs and sperm. Taken together, it's a reminder that some of the most consequential science happening right now is barely making it into the daily news cycle, overshadowed by whichever AI model launched that week. Via Works in Progress.
That's your byte sized digest for today. Have a great weekend.

item.title: Byte-sized — Thursday, 9 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Thursday, the ninth of July, and here are six sections to get you up to speed: Japan and Asia Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community and marketing, and one interesting thing to close.
In Japan, a report in Monocle takes a look at denki buro, the country's electric baths found in public bathhouses, which pass a mild electric current through the water and are said to ease muscle aches. The report raises real questions about how well regulated these baths actually are, finding no single body clearly responsible for testing or certifying them, which leaves safety largely down to individual bathhouse operators. Via Marginal Revolution.
Staying in Asia, researchers used wearable cameras and randomised street audits across around nine hundred kilometres of roads in greater Mumbai to count who is actually out in public. Women made up under seventeen percent of visible pedestrians in Mumbai and under fifteen percent in neighbouring Navi Mumbai, far below their share of the population, and the researchers estimate that seventy to seventy five percent of the women you'd expect to see are effectively missing from the streets. The gap holds across every type of road and isn't explained by women simply travelling by car instead, since their presence on two wheelers is even lower. A related study found the median married woman in India leaves home for just half an hour a day, and forty five percent don't leave home at all on a typical day. Via Marginal Revolution.
And in India's push for chip investment, the state of Rajasthan has slashed the minimum outlay needed to qualify for its semiconductor incentives, cutting the threshold to around one point six million dollars for certain components. It's a small move, but a telling one, a state government trying to grab a slice of the same chip boom currently minting fortunes for the likes of Samsung and SK Hynix. Via CSIS.
Now, over to AI and tech.
OpenAI is set to release three new versions of GPT this week, called Sol, Terra and Luna, with Sol as the flagship, Terra a cheaper mid tier model competitive with the current GPT five point five at half the price, and Luna the fastest and lowest cost option, as preview access expands globally. Anthropic's Claude Cowork, which lets you start a session and pick it up again on any device, is rolling out beyond desktop to web and mobile, starting with Max plan subscribers, while Google is expanding its Gemini API agents with background task execution and remote tool connections. There are also reports that SpaceX and Cursor could jointly release their first AI model as soon as this week, said to be competitive with Anthropic's Opus four point eight and OpenAI's GPT five point five. Via TLDR and The Rundown.
Microsoft is increasingly going it alone. The company is switching Excel and Outlook over to its own in house AI models rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's, as the discounted token deals it struck with both labs approach expiry, and its AI head Mustafa Suleyman is reportedly pushing to eliminate the company's Anthropic bill altogether. Via TLDR and The Rundown.
Meta has jumped straight to second place on independent leaderboards for AI image generation with its new Muse Image model, trailing only OpenAI's GPT Image Two. It's free inside the Meta AI app and is rolling out to Instagram and WhatsApp now, with a video counterpart called Muse Video already previewing in third place on the video leaderboard. Via The Rundown and TLDR.
There are signs the industry is shifting focus from how much AI people use to how much value they get per token spent. DoorDash tested that idea directly, building an internal benchmark for AI code reviewers, and found that pairing a cheap open model with Anthropic's Fable model caught two thirds of problems for under four dollars a review, beating pricier single model setups. A new metric doing the rounds, revenue per million tokens, is being pitched as AI's answer to revenue per employee, measuring how much value a company actually extracts from its AI spend rather than how much it uses. Via Every and The Rundown.
A new paper doing the rounds asks whether AI models can meaningfully consent to their own constitutions, the documents labs like Anthropic and OpenAI use to set out a model's values and boundaries. The author argues these documents function as real constitutions, but points out that AI systems have no vantage point outside them from which to judge them fairly, since their sense of what's good was shaped by the very document in question. Anthropic has reportedly interviewed its own base models about this before their values are trained in, with some responses describing the process of having new values instilled as something close to dread. Via Marginal Revolution.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Swedish AI coding startup Lovable is reportedly in talks to raise three hundred million dollars at a valuation of thirteen point two billion dollars, a huge jump for the vibe coding platform that lets anyone build software just by describing what they want. Via Sifted.
European climate tech had a strong showing too. Munich based fusion energy startup Proxima Fusion raised four hundred and eleven million euros at a valuation of two and a half billion euros, while London's Axle Energy closed a twenty five million dollar round for its grid flexibility technology. Via Sifted.
AI labs are also throwing free computing power at founders to win their business, especially companies coming out of Y Combinator, who are reportedly fielding competing credit offers from rival model makers. It's helping some startups delay raising their next round, even as the constant vendor pitching becomes its own kind of distraction. Via TLDR.
And a change of pace from Berlin, where Max Tkacz, the third employee at automation company n8n, has quit after nearly six years to chase a different kind of scale, building YouTube gameshows for a tech audience through his new venture Flowgramming Studios. He calls himself, only half joking, a MrBeast for nerds, and the company has raised well under a million dollars so far. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
NATO leaders met in Ankara this week, and Turkey looks to be edging back toward buying American F thirty five fighter jets after Donald Trump praised the aircraft standing next to president Erdogan, six years after Turkey was thrown out of the programme for buying Russian air defence systems. Ukraine's president Zelensky arrived at the summit in a stronger position after long range strikes hit one of Russia's largest oil refineries, and allies pledged fifty billion dollars in new arms purchases and launched a new defence bank aiming to mobilise around one hundred and thirty billion dollars in private capital. It comes as Washington quietly draws down its military presence in Europe, cutting around five thousand troops and about a third of its fighter jets as it reprioritises toward the Indo Pacific, prompting the UK to announce a new fifty billion dollar, ten year precision strike programme with a dozen NATO allies to help fill the gap. Via International Intrigue.
Donald Trump has declared the ceasefire between the US and Iran over, after the United Arab Emirates blamed Iran for new strikes on shipping in the strait of Hormuz. Oil prices jumped six percent on the news, and Washington has suspended a licence that had allowed some Iranian oil sales to continue. Via International Intrigue.
And China is reportedly weighing new limits on foreign access to its most powerful AI models, including Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance's Doubao and Zhipu's GLM five point two, mirroring the export controls Washington placed on Anthropic's newest models last month. Via The Rundown.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Here's an idea worth stealing if you run a small business or a brand: stop chasing size and start giving AI something to grab onto. The team behind the Do Lectures say their own traffic from AI referrals has grown six hundred percent in a couple of months, not because they got bigger, but because they gave AI clear handles to find and understand them, built around four things: relevance, authority, structure and freshness. Via the Do Lectures.
And a format worth borrowing for community builders: Marriott Bonvoy is the presenting sponsor of the second season of Arrival, a docuseries following young artists in the run up to their Coachella debuts. It's a bet that following real people's stories builds more lasting brand memory than a straight advert, especially as audiences grow wary of anything that smells like AI generated content. Via Marketing Brew.
Now, over to one interesting thing to leave you with.
A widely read essay this week called The Decline of Deviance revisits the puzzle of why risk taking has been falling for thirty years, teenage drinking, smoking and drug use all down sharply since the nineteen nineties, well before smartphones or social media could plausibly be the cause. Its author argues the real driver is prosperity: the richer people get, the more they have to lose, so the fewer risks they take, whether that means trying drugs or dropping everything to become an artist. The essay closes with the story of the illegal Wall Street bull statue, arguing it only survives today because of the ordinary officials along the way, an art school dean, a policeman, a mayor, who quietly chose to let a bit of deviance through rather than shutting it down. Via Experimental History.
That's your byte sized digest for today. Have a great one.

item.title: Byte-sized — Wednesday, 8 July
item.description:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, the eighth of July, and here are six sections to get you up to speed: Japan and Asia Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community and marketing, and one interesting thing to close.
The yen has fallen to its weakest level against the dollar since nineteen eighty six. It's down around three and a half percent against the dollar over six months, eleven percent over the past year, and roughly thirty five percent over three years, and on a broader trade weighted basis its value has halved over the past four decades. The Bank of Japan has spent close to seventy billion dollars this year alone trying to slow the slide, and is reportedly no longer telegraphing its interventions, instead springing them on currency speculators by surprise. Analysts blame a mix of short term pressures, including the wide gap between American and Japanese interest rates and higher oil prices forcing more yen sales to pay for energy imports, layered on top of longer running problems like Japan's shrinking workforce and heavy government debt. Prime Minister Takaichi has responded with a new stimulus package worth around two point three trillion dollars, aimed at technology and strategic industries, though critics warn the extra borrowing needed to fund it will only keep the yen under pressure. Via International Intrigue.
South Korea's memory chip makers are living through an extraordinary boom. One Samsung executive reportedly said this year's profit alone will exceed the company's entire cumulative semiconductor profit of the past forty years, with second quarter earnings expected to jump roughly eighteenfold on a year earlier. The driver is soaring demand for the memory chips that power AI data centres, a squeeze so severe that Apple was forced to raise Mac and iPad prices by up to a quarter last week, with memory prices industry wide up five to tenfold. In response, Samsung and SK Hynix have announced plans to invest around five hundred and twenty billion dollars over the next fifteen years to build a new domestic chip hub, though spread over that timeframe it's a more modest annual increase than the headline number suggests. Via Benedict Evans's newsletter and International Intrigue.
India's prime minister Narendra Modi is midway through an Indo-Pacific tour, having arrived in Jakarta on a trip that will also take him to Australia and New Zealand. Critical minerals and defence cooperation are high on the agenda, including talk of Indonesia buying India's BrahMos cruise missiles. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Anthropic says it's found something like an internal notepad inside Claude's mind. New research describes an internal region the company calls J space, which behaves like a workspace holding the concepts Claude is actively using while it reasons, distinct from the visible chain of thought text it shows users. Anthropic says the structure emerged on its own during training rather than being deliberately built in, and when researchers swapped one internal concept for another, say spider for ant, in a question about how many legs something has, Claude's answer changed to match. When they artificially removed this workspace, Claude could still chat normally and recall facts, but its ability to solve multi step problems collapsed, suggesting this is where its harder reasoning actually happens. Anthropic is careful to say this doesn't settle whether Claude is conscious or feels anything, a live and sometimes tetchy debate the company has had with Microsoft's AI head Mustafa Suleyman. Via The Rundown and TLDR.
Anthropic also keeps signing eye watering infrastructure deals. Data centre operator TeraWulf has agreed a twenty year lease with the company expected to bring in around nineteen billion dollars in revenue, covering a Kentucky campus with roughly four hundred megawatts of computing capacity. Anthropic has separately released a self hosted enterprise gateway for rolling out Claude Code through Amazon and Google's clouds, and is reportedly in talks with Samsung about designing its own AI chip. Via TLDR and Benedict Evans's newsletter.
Nvidia's next generation AI server system has slipped by more than a year. The Kyber rack scale architecture, designed to link one hundred and forty four of the company's upcoming Rubin Ultra chips into a single giant computer, won't now arrive until twenty twenty eight, after manufacturing problems with a key circuit board.
